summary:
THEIA used three NASA Image and Video Library resources documenting astronaut exercise aboard the International Space Station: Frank Rubio's treadmill exercise, astronaut Hopkins' ARED exercise, and Suni Williams' ARED training.

These recordings provided authentic spaceflight exercise references for exploring movement analysis under microgravity conditions.

Our movement-analysis architecture uses Sapiens2-1B for 2D pose estimation, a standardized 17-joint representation, and one-second temporal windows. It combines supervised movement classification with regional density-based deviation detection to identify unusual movement patterns and support visual review.

The NASA resources helped connect our rehabilitation-focused research with astronaut exercise scenarios, informing THEIA Space's approach to monitoring movement quality and potential compensations.
details:
THEIA — Movement Intelligence for Earth & Space

THEIA tells adaptation from maladaptation and coaches people to move better, from the rehabilitation room to the space station.

THEIA is a research-driven movement intelligence system that combines scientific research, a custom AI analysis architecture, and two connected applications: one for astronauts in space and one for people undergoing physical rehabilitation on Earth.

Scientific Research & NASA Resources

We explored a fundamental challenge in astronaut health monitoring: how can we distinguish healthy adaptation to microgravity from potentially harmful movement compensations when conventional Earth-based movement baselines no longer apply?

Our research identified a parallel between astronauts adapting to microgravity and people relearning to walk after injuries, including individuals undergoing prosthetic rehabilitation.

We integrated NASA astronaut exercise references with rehabilitation movement research to investigate whether clinically meaningful movement patterns from Earth could improve movement assessment in space.

We used NASA's publicly available treadmill and Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED) footage to study astronaut movement scenarios in microgravity. NASA Human Research Program resources informed our understanding of sensorimotor adaptation, musculoskeletal deconditioning, physical performance risks, and existing exercise countermeasures.

Custom AI Model & Dataset Research

We developed a custom movement-analysis architecture combining Sapiens2-1B pose estimation, standardized 17-joint representations, temporal feature extraction, supervised classification, and regional density-based deviation detection.

Our approach integrates two complementary analytical methods:

  • Supervised movement analysis: identifies movement patterns using pose and geometric features.
  • Regional deviation detection: identifies unusual movement patterns through statistical analysis of movement characteristics across body regions.

We incorporated the ProGait rehabilitation dataset and its gait annotations into our research, connecting movement patterns from prosthetic rehabilitation with astronaut exercise monitoring.

Our initial experiments explored whether rehabilitation data could improve the identification of movement compensations. This work also revealed a critical limitation: the scarcity of clinically labeled adaptation data.

This discovery shaped the next stage of THEIA.

All the details are included in a whitepaper on our website.

THEIA Space — Astronaut Application

THEIA Space is designed to analyze astronaut movement during physical exercise and provide actionable feedback on movement quality.

The proposed application uses video-based movement analysis to identify emerging compensatory patterns, monitor changes over time, and support decisions about exercise technique.

Our long-term objective is to help distinguish beneficial adaptation to microgravity from potentially harmful changes in movement mechanics, supporting safer and more effective exercise.

THEIA Earth — Rehabilitation Application

THEIA Earth is designed for people undergoing physical rehabilitation, including individuals with mobility impairments and those learning to walk with prosthetics.

The application aims to provide accessible movement feedback while enabling longitudinal collection of rehabilitation movement data.

With appropriate consent and clinical oversight, these recordings can help create a growing dataset of movement adaptations, compensatory strategies, and rehabilitation progress.

THEIA Earth is both a rehabilitation support tool and a potential source of clinically meaningful movement data for improving THEIA Space.

Early Traction & Community Validation

To test public interest in the problem and build an initial audience for THEIA Earth, we launched an Instagram content initiative explaining the connection between rehabilitation and astronaut movement adaptation.

Our content generated over 6,500 views within the first few hours.

This early engagement demonstrates initial audience reach and provides a starting point for recruiting rehabilitation participants, engaging clinical professionals, and expanding our future movement-data collection initiative.

Intended Impact

THEIA connects two environments where the human body must learn new ways to move.

Our vision is to create a continuous learning system: rehabilitation data from Earth informs movement intelligence for astronauts, while advances in movement analysis can contribute to better rehabilitation tools on Earth.

By combining NASA research, clinically informed movement datasets, custom AI models, and applications designed for both environments, THEIA aims to transform movement monitoring from simple exercise tracking into adaptation-aware movement intelligence.
